title: How Much Energy Does Building Distro Packages Use
excerpt: Some metrics When I set up the infrastructure for Casuarina Linux I repurposed an AMD AM4 system with Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core CPU (105W TDP) and 32Gb of DDR4 RAM as the build server. I set it up in our laundry, connected it via a smart plug, and reset its counters. content_html:
When I set up the infrastructure for Casuarina Linux I repurposed an AMD AM4 system with Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core CPU (105W TDP) and 32Gb of DDR4 RAM as the build server. I set it up in our laundry, connected it via a smart plug, and reset its counters. Over the course of the project I would regularly pull package updates from Chimera Linux, build and install them locally, and then push them to the repo, which would trigger Buildbot to build and publish them.

The project ran from 30 March 2026 to 8 November 2026 (a bit over 7 months) the total energy used was 98.4 kWh. My electricity plan is a 100% renewable plan (meaning they offset the non-renewable parts) and costs AU$0.33 kWh. Ignoring the daily service fee the cost of that electricity is AU$32.47 .

Since it turned out I was the only one doing package updates I kept the builder off when idle. When there were packages to build I’d hit the power button (on the machine, not the smart plug) and some time later when it was done I’d press it again to shut it down. This was pretty beneficial as the idle draw was about 55W.

The number of package builds was around 5000. SELECT COUNT(name) FROM logs WHERE name LIKE 'pkg:%'; from the Buildbot state.sqlite yields 5201, however that’s probably slightly inflated due to rebuilds/packages that failed to build on the first try.

The actual usage is likely more than double the 98kWh figure as all packages were built on my desktop machine first, before pushing to the repository for the builder to pick up. That machine is an AM5 system with AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core CPU (170W TDP), 64Gb DDR5 RAM. Additionally our house has rooftop solar, and where possible I would kick off builds during the day so there was a better chance of using the solar. That would have reduced the actual cost, but I have no way to measure the specific amount.

The slowest package by far to build was Chromium, taking just shy of 4 hours to complete. For comparison Firefox takes about 50 minutes. Power draw measured by the smart plug when the builder was fully loaded is about 193W. So 4 hours at 193W is 0.77kWh, which means a Chromium build costs about 25 cents.

Overall it cost a bit under AU$5 a month (ignoring solar, and my workstation) to build all the packages for a Linux distribution. That’s not too bad I think.
